title: V. By Ilusha’s Bedside
paragraphs: The room occupied by the family of the retired captain Snegiryov is already familiar to the reader. At that moment it was close and crowded with visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha, and though they were all ready, like Smurov, to deny that Alyosha had brought them and reconciled them with Ilusha, the fact was that he had. All the artistry he had used was to lead each of them to Ilusha one by one, without any “sheepish sentimentality,” appearing to do so casually and without any plan. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. He was deeply moved by the almost tender affection and sympathy shown him by these boys who had once been his enemies. Krassotkin was the only one still missing, and his absence weighed heavily on Ilusha's heart. Of all his bitter memories, perhaps the most bitter was having stabbed Krassotkin, who had been his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, the first to make it up with Ilusha, thought so too. But when Smurov hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come and see him about something, the latter cut him off, telling Smurov to inform “Karamazov” right then that he knew best what to do, that he didn't need anyone's advice, and that if he went to see Ilusha, he'd choose his own time — he had “his own reasons.”

That was a fortnight before this Sunday. That's why Alyosha hadn't come himself, as he had intended. But even as he waited, he sent Smurov to him twice more. Both times Krassotkin met him with a curt, impatient refusal, sending Alyosha the message to stop bothering him, and that if Alyosha came in person, Krassotkin would refuse to go to Ilusha at all. Right up to the last day, Smurov didn't know that Kolya meant to visit Ilusha that morning — only on the evening before, as he parted from Smurov, did Kolya abruptly tell him to wait at home for him next morning, because they'd go to the Snegiryovs' together; but he warned him on no account to say he was coming, as he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov's notion that Kolya would bring back the lost dog was based on words Kolya had dropped — that “they must be asses not to find the dog, if it was alive.” When Smurov, watching for an opportunity, timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. “I'm not such an ass as to go hunting around town for other people's dogs when I've got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could still be alive after swallowing a pin? Sheepish sentimentality, that's what it is!”

For the last fortnight Ilusha had not left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He had not been at school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He had fallen ill the same day, though for a month afterward he was sometimes able to get up and walk about the room and the passage. But lately he had grown so weak that he couldn't move without his father's help. His father was terribly worried about him. He even gave up drinking and was nearly out of his mind with terror that his boy might die. Often, especially after leading him around the room on his arm and putting him back to bed, he would run to a dark corner of the passage and, pressing his head against the wall, break into fits of violent weeping, stifling his sobs so Ilusha wouldn't hear.

Coming back into the room, he would usually start doing something to amuse and comfort his precious boy — telling him stories, funny anecdotes, or mimicking comic people he happened to have met, even imitating the howls and cries of animals. But Ilusha couldn't bear to see his father fooling and playing the buffoon. Though the boy tried not to show how much he disliked it, he saw with an aching heart that his father was an object of contempt, and he was constantly haunted by the memory of the “wisp of tow” and that “terrible day.”

Nina, Ilusha's gentle, crippled sister, did not like her father's buffoonery either (Varvara had been gone some time now to Petersburg to study at the university). But the half-witted mother was greatly entertained and laughed heartily when her husband began capering about or performing some routine. It was the only way she could be amused; the rest of the time she was grumbling and complaining that everyone had forgotten her, that no one treated her with respect, that she was being slighted, and so on. Lately, though, she had changed completely. She had begun gazing constantly at Ilusha's bed in the corner and seemed lost in thought. She had grown more silent, quieter, and, if she cried, she cried quietly so as not to be heard. The captain noticed the change in her with mournful perplexity. The boys' visits had at first only angered her, but later on their cheerful shouts and stories began to divert her, and at last she grew so fond of them that, if the boys had stopped coming, she would have felt miserable without them. When the children told some story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She would call some of them over and kiss them. She was especially fond of Smurov.

As for the captain, the presence in his room of the children who came to cheer up Ilusha filled his heart from the first with ecstatic joy. He even hoped that Ilusha would now shake off his low spirits, and that this would speed his recovery. Despite his alarm about Ilusha, he had not, until very recently, felt even a moment's doubt that the boy would ultimately recover.

He welcomed his little visitors with deference, waited on them hand and foot; he was ready to be their horse and even started letting them ride on his back, but Ilusha didn't like the game and it was given up. He began buying them little things — gingerbread and nuts — gave them tea, and made them sandwiches. It must be noted that he had plenty of money all this time. He had taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, exactly as Alyosha had predicted. And afterward Katerina Ivanovna, learning more about their circumstances and Ilusha's illness, had visited them herself, gotten to know the family, and succeeded in charming the half-witted mother. Since then she had been lavish in helping them, and the captain, terrified that his boy might be dying, forgot his pride and humbly accepted her assistance.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, sent for by Katerina Ivanovna, had been coming punctually every other day, but little was gained from his visits, and he dosed the invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, who had come from Moscow where he had a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at great expense, not specifically for Ilusha, but for another purpose which will be explained in its proper place. Since he had come, she had asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had no idea that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, even though he had long hoped for a visit from the boy Ilusha was fretting over.

At the moment Krassotkin opened the door and stepped into the room, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha's bed, looking at a tiny mastiff puppy that had been born only the day before. The captain had spoken for it a week ago, hoping to comfort and amuse Ilusha, who was still grieving over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Ilusha, who had heard three days earlier that he was to be presented with a puppy — not just any puppy, but a pedigreed mastiff (a very important detail, of course) — had tried, out of delicacy of feeling, to pretend to be pleased. But his father and the boys could see plainly that the puppy only recalled to his little heart the unhappy dog he had killed. The puppy lay next to him, moving feebly, and he, smiling sadly, stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand. He clearly liked the puppy, but ... it wasn't Zhutchka. If he could have had Zhutchka and the puppy, then he would have been completely happy.
“Krassotkin!” one of the boys cried out suddenly. He was the first to notice him come in.
Krassotkin's entrance caused a general stir; the boys stepped back and stood on either side of the bed so that he could get a full view of Ilusha. The captain rushed eagerly to meet Kolya.
“Please come in ... you are most welcome!” he said hurriedly. “Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!”

But Krassotkin, shaking hands with him hurriedly, immediately demonstrated his complete grasp of polite society's manners. He turned first to the captain's wife, sitting in her armchair — who was in an ill humor just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha's bed, keeping her from seeing the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he made her a bow, scraping his foot, and then turning to Nina, he made her, as the only other lady present, an identical bow. This polite behavior made an extremely favorable impression on the deranged lady.
“There, you can see at once he's a young man who's been well brought up,” she commented aloud, throwing up her hands. “But as for our other visitors, they come piling in one on top of another.”
“How do you mean, mamma, one on top of another — how is that?” the captain muttered affectionately, though a little anxious on her account.
“That's how they ride in. They climb up on each other's shoulders in the passage and come prancing in on a respectable family. Strange sort of visitors!”
“But who's come in that way, mamma?”
“Why, that boy came in riding on that one's back, and this one was on that one's.”

Kolya was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy turned visibly paler. He raised himself up in bed and gazed intently at Kolya. Kolya had not seen his little friend for two months, and he was struck at the sight of him. He had never imagined he would see such a wasted, yellow face, such enormous, feverishly burning eyes, such thin little hands. With grieved surprise he saw Ilusha's rapid, labored breathing and dry lips. He stepped close, held out his hand, and, almost overcome, said:

“Well, old man ... how are you?” But his voice failed him; he couldn't quite carry off an easy manner; his face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth quivered. Ilusha gave him a pitiful little smile, still unable to utter a word. Something moved Kolya to raise his hand and run it over Ilusha's hair.
“Never mind!” he murmured softly to him, to cheer him up, or perhaps not knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
“Hello — so you've got a new puppy?” Kolya said suddenly, in his most unfeeling voice.
“Ye—es,” Ilusha answered in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

“Black nose — that means he'll be fierce, a good house dog,” Kolya observed gravely and stolidly, as if the puppy and its black nose were the only thing on his mind. In reality, he was still doing his utmost to control his feelings and not burst out crying like a child, and try as he might he couldn't quite master them. “When he grows up, you'll have to keep him on a chain, I'm sure.”
“He'll be a huge dog!” one of the boys cried.
“Of course he will,” “a mastiff,” “big,” “like this,” “as big as a calf,” several voices shouted.

“As big as a calf, as a real calf,” the captain chimed in. “I got one like that on purpose, one of the fiercest breeds; his parents are huge and very fierce, they stand this high from the floor. Sit down here, on Ilusha's bed, or here on the bench. You are most welcome; we've been hoping to see you for a long time. You were kind enough to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Krassotkin sat down on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha's feet. Though on the way he had perhaps prepared a free and easy opening for the conversation, he now completely lost his thread.

“No ... I came with Perezvon. I've got a dog now, called Perezvon. A Slavonic name. He's out there ... if I whistle, he'll come running in. I've brought a dog too,” he said, suddenly addressing Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?” he suddenly fired the question at him.

Ilusha's little face quivered. He looked at Kolya with an agonized expression. Alyosha, standing at the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to speak of Zhutchka, but Kolya didn't see it, or pretended not to.
“Where ... is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked in a broken voice.
“Oh, well, my boy, your Zhutchka is lost and done for!”
Ilusha didn't speak, but he fixed an intent gaze on Kolya once more. Alyosha caught Kolya's eye and signaled to him vigorously again, but Kolya turned his eyes away, pretending not to have noticed.

“She must have run off and died somewhere. She was bound to die after a meal like that,” Kolya pronounced pitilessly, though he seemed a little breathless. “But I've got a dog, Perezvon ... A Slavonic name. I've brought him to show you.”
“I don't want him!” Ilusha said suddenly.

“No, no, you really must see him ... he'll amuse you. I brought him on purpose. He's the same sort of shaggy dog. Will you allow me to call in my dog, madam?” He suddenly turned to Madame Snegiryov, with inexplicable excitement in his manner.
“I don't want him, I don't want him!” cried Ilusha, with a mournful break in his voice. There was a reproachful light in his eyes.

“You'd better,” said the captain, starting up from the chest by the wall where he had just sat down, “you'd better ... another time,” he muttered, but Kolya could not be held back. He hurriedly shouted to Smurov, “Open the door,” and as soon as it was open, he blew his whistle. Perezvon came rushing headlong into the room.

“Jump, Perezvon, beg! Beg!” Kolya shouted, springing up, and the dog rose on his hind legs by Ilusha's bedside. What happened next took everyone by surprise: Ilusha started, lurched violently forward, bent over Perezvon, and gazed at him, faint with suspense.
“It's ... Zhutchka!” he cried suddenly, in a voice breaking with joy and suffering.
“And who did you think it was?” Krassotkin shouted at the top of his voice, in a ringing, joyful tone, and bending down he seized the dog and lifted him up to Ilusha.

“Look, old man — you see, blind in one eye and the left ear torn, just the marks you described to me. That's how I found him. I found him right away. He didn't belong to anyone!” he explained, turning quickly to the captain, to his wife, to Alyosha, and back to Ilusha. “He used to hang around the Fedotovs' back yard. Though he made his home there, they never fed him. He was a stray that had wandered in from the village. I found him. You see, old man, he couldn't have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he would have died — he'd have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he's alive. You didn't see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue — that's why he yelped. He ran off yelping, and you thought he'd swallowed it. He would have yelped, of course, because the skin of a dog's mouth is so tender ... tenderer than in a person, much tenderer!” Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing and radiant with delight. Ilusha couldn't speak. White as a sheet, he gazed open-mouthed at Kolya, his great eyes almost bulging out of his head. And if Krassotkin, who had no suspicion of it, had known what a disastrous and fatal effect such a moment might have on the sick child's health, nothing would have induced him to pull such a stunt on him. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who grasped it. As for the captain, he was behaving like a little child.
“Zhutchka! It's Zhutchka!” he cried in a blissful voice. “Ilusha, this is Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, this is Zhutchka!” He was almost weeping.
“And I never guessed!” Smurov cried regretfully. “Bravo, Krassotkin! I said he'd find the dog, and here he's found him.”
“Here he's found him!” another boy repeated joyfully.
“Krassotkin's a champion!” a third voice cried.
“He's a champion, he's a champion!” the other boys cried, and began clapping.

“Hold on, hold on,” Krassotkin did his best to shout over them all. “I'll tell you how it happened, that's the whole point. I found him, I took him home and hid him right away. I kept him locked up at home and didn't show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov has known for the last fortnight, but I assured him the dog was called Perezvon and he didn't guess. Meanwhile I've been teaching the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog in fine shape, old man, so I could say to you, ‘See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!' Haven't you got a bit of meat? He'll show you a trick that'll make you die laughing. A piece of meat — have you got any?”

The captain ran across the passage to the landlady, where their cooking was done. So as not to waste precious time, Kolya, in desperate haste, shouted to Perezvon, “Dead!” And the dog immediately turned over and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the person most delighted by the dog's performance was “mamma.” She laughed at the dog and began snapping her fingers and calling it, “Perezvon, Perezvon!”

“Nothing will make him get up, nothing!” Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. “He won't move for any shouting in the world, but if I call him, he'll jump up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!” The dog sprang up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain came running back with a piece of cooked beef.

“Is it hot?” Kolya asked hurriedly, with a businesslike air, taking the meat. “Dogs don't like hot things. No, it's fine. Look, everyone, look, Ilusha, look, old man — why aren't you looking? He does not look at him, now that I've brought him.”

The new trick consisted in making the dog stand motionless with his nose out, while a tempting morsel of meat was balanced on the tip of his nose. The luckless dog had to stand without moving, the meat on his nose, as long as his master chose to keep him there — without a movement, perhaps for half an hour. But he held Perezvon only a brief moment.
“Paid for!” Kolya cried, and the meat flashed from the dog's nose to his mouth. The audience, of course, expressed enthusiasm and surprise.
“Can you really have put off coming all this time just to train the dog?” Alyosha exclaimed, with an involuntary note of reproach in his voice.
“Just for that!” Kolya answered, with perfect simplicity. “I wanted to show him off in all his glory.”
“Perezvon! Perezvon!” called Ilusha suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

“What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!” Kolya slapped the bed and Perezvon darted up next to Ilusha. The boy threw both arms around his head and Perezvon instantly licked his cheek. Ilusha pressed close against him, stretched himself out in bed, and buried his face in the dog's shaggy coat.
“Dear, dear!” the captain kept exclaiming. Kolya sat down again on the edge of the bed.
“Ilusha, I can show you another trick. I've brought you a little cannon. Remember, I told you about it before and you said how much you'd like to see it. Well — here, I've brought it to you.”

And Kolya hurriedly pulled out of his satchel the little bronze cannon. He hurried because he was happy himself. Another time he would have waited until the sensation made by Perezvon had worn off; now he hurried on without a thought for any of that. “You're all happy now,” he felt, “so here's something to make you happier!” He was himself utterly enchanted.

“I've been coveting this thing for a long time. It's for you, old man, it's for you. It belonged to Morozov; it was no use to him, he had it from his brother. I traded a book from father's bookcase for it — _A Kinsman of Mahomet, or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book printed in Moscow a hundred years ago, before they had any censorship. And Morozov has a taste for such things. He was grateful to me, too.”

Kolya held the cannon in his hand so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha raised himself up, and, with his right arm still around the dog, he gazed at the toy in enchantment. The sensation was even greater when Kolya announced that he had gunpowder, too, and that it could be fired off right then “if it won't alarm the ladies.” “Mamma” immediately asked to see the toy up close and her request was granted. She was much pleased with the little bronze cannon on wheels and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She readily gave permission for the cannon to be fired, without any idea what she had been asked. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, as an old military man, undertook to load it, putting in a tiny bit of powder. He asked that the shot be put off for another time. The cannon was set on the floor, aimed at an empty part of the room; three grains of powder were thrust into the touchhole and a match was put to it. A magnificent explosion followed. Mamma was startled, but at once laughed with delight. The boys gazed in speechless triumph. But the captain, looking at Ilusha, was more enchanted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and immediately presented it to Ilusha, along with the powder and the shot.
“I got it for you, for you! I've been keeping it for you a long time,” he repeated once more, in his delight.
“Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!” mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn't get it. Kolya was disconcerted. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

“Mamma, mamma,” he ran to her, “the cannon is yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, because it's a present to him, but it's just as good as yours. Ilusha will always let you play with it; it shall belong to both of you, both of you.”
“No, I don't want it to belong to both of us, I want it to be mine alone, not Ilusha's,” mamma persisted, on the verge of tears.

“Take it, mother, here, keep it!” Ilusha cried. “Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?” He turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as though afraid he might be offended at his giving his present to someone else.
“Of course you may,” Krassotkin agreed heartily, and, taking the cannon from Ilusha, he handed it to mamma himself with a polite bow. She was so moved she began to cry.
“Ilusha, darling — he's the one who loves his mamma!” she said tenderly, and at once began wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
“Mamma, let me kiss your hand.” The captain darted over to her at once and did so.
“And I've never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy,” said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

“And I'll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make the powder ourselves now. Borovikov found out how it's done — twenty-four parts of saltpeter, ten of sulfur, and six of birchwood charcoal. It's all pounded together, mixed into a paste with water, and rubbed through a tammy sieve — that's how it's done.”
“Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it's not real gunpowder,” Ilusha answered.
“Not real?” Kolya flushed. “It burns. I don't know, of course.”
“No, I didn't mean that,” the captain put in with a guilty face. “I only said that real powder isn't made like that, but that's nothing — it can be made that way.”

“I don't know, you know best. We lit some of it in a pomatum pot; it burned splendidly, all of it burned away leaving only a tiny bit of ash. But that was just the paste, and if you rub it through a sieve ... well, of course you know best, I don't know. And Bulkin's father thrashed him on account of our powder — did you hear?” he said, turning to Ilusha.
“Yes,” Ilusha answered. He listened to Kolya with enormous interest and enjoyment.

“We had prepared a whole bottle of it, and he used to keep it under his bed. His father saw it. He said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to lodge a complaint against me with the masters. He's not allowed to hang around with me now; no one is allowed to hang around with me now. Smurov isn't allowed to either. I've got a bad name with everyone. They say I'm a ‘desperate character,'” Kolya smiled scornfully. “It all started with what happened on the railway.”

“Ah, we've heard of that exploit of yours too,” the captain cried. “How could you lie still on the rails? Were you really not the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren't you frightened?”
The captain was positively abject in his flattery of Kolya.

“N-not particularly,” Kolya answered casually. “What's blasted my reputation more than anything here was that cursed goose,” he said, turning again to Ilusha. But though he assumed an unconcerned air as he talked, he still couldn't quite control himself and kept missing the note he tried to hit.
“Ah, I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. “They told me, but I didn't understand. Did they really take you to the court?”

“The most stupid, trivial affair — they made a mountain of a molehill, as they always do,” Kolya began casually. “I was walking through the marketplace here one day, just when they'd driven the geese in. I stopped and looked at them. All at once a fellow, who works as an errand boy at Plotnikov's now, looked at me and said, ‘What are you looking at the geese for?' I looked at him: a stupid, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I'm always on the side of the peasantry, you know. I like talking to peasants. We've fallen behind the peasants — that's an axiom. I believe you're laughing, Karamazov?”
“No, Heaven forbid — I'm listening,” Alyosha said with a most good-natured air, and the sensitive Kolya was immediately reassured.

“My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple,” he hurried on again, looking pleased. “I believe in the people and am always happy to give them their due, but I'm not for spoiling them — that's a _sine qua non_ ... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and answered, ‘I'm wondering what the goose is thinking about.' He looked at me quite stupidly. ‘And what's the goose thinking about?' he asked. ‘Do you see that cart full of oats?' I said. ‘The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has stuck its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up — do you see?' ‘I see that quite clearly,' he said. ‘Well,' said I, ‘if that cart were to move forward just a little, would it break the goose's neck or not?' ‘It'd be sure to break it' — and he grinned all over his face, highly delighted. ‘Come on, then,' said I, ‘let's try.' ‘Let's,' he said. And it didn't take us long to arrange: he stood at the bridle without being noticed, and I stood on the other side to direct the goose. The owner wasn't looking, he was talking to someone, so I had nothing to do — the goose thrust its head in after the oats on its own, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he tugged at the bridle, and crack! The goose's neck was broken in half. And, as luck would have it, all the peasants saw us at that moment, and they kicked up a row on the spot. ‘You did that on purpose!' ‘No, not on purpose.' ‘Yes, you did, on purpose!' Well, they shouted, ‘Take him to the justice of the peace!' They took me along too. ‘You were there,' they said, ‘you helped, you're known all over the market!' And, for some reason, I really am known all over the market,” Kolya added conceitedly. “We all went off to the justice's; they brought the goose along as well. The fellow was crying, in a dreadful funk, simply blubbering like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting that you could kill any number of geese that way. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice of the peace settled it in a minute: the farmer was to be paid a rouble for the goose, and the fellow was to have the goose. And he was warned not to pull pranks like that again. And the fellow kept blubbering like a woman. ‘It wasn't me,' he said, ‘it was he who egged me on,' and he pointed to me. I answered with the utmost composure that I hadn't egged him on, that I had simply stated the general proposition, had spoken hypothetically. The justice of the peace smiled, and was vexed with himself for it at once. ‘I'll complain to your masters,' he said, ‘so that in future you won't waste your time on such general propositions instead of sitting with your books and learning your lessons.' He didn't complain to the masters — that was a joke — but the matter was noised about and came to the masters' ears. Their ears are long, you know! The classics master, Kolbasnikov, was particularly shocked about it, but Dardanelov got me off again. But Kolbasnikov is savage with everyone now like a raw ass. Did you know, Ilusha, he's just been married — got a dowry of a thousand roubles — and his bride is a regular fright of the first rank and the last degree. The third-class fellows wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.

And so on — awfully funny, I'll bring it to you later. I don't say anything against Dardanelov; he's a learned man, no doubt about it. I respect men like that, and it's not because he stood up for me.”
“But you took him down a peg about the founders of Troy!” Smurov suddenly put in, unmistakably proud of Krassotkin at that moment. He was especially pleased with the story of the goose.
“Did you really take him down?” the captain inquired in a flattering tone. “On the question of who founded Troy? We heard about that — Ilusha told me at the time.”
“He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” Ilusha put in. “He only pretends to be like that, but really he's top of the class in every subject.”
Ilusha looked at Kolya with infinite happiness.

“Oh, that's all nonsense about Troy, a trivial matter. I consider it an unimportant question,” Kolya said with haughty humility. By now he had completely recovered his dignity, though he was still a little uneasy. He felt he had been greatly excited and had talked about the goose, for instance, with too little reserve, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn't said a word the whole time. And the vain boy began gradually to feel a nagging fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him, thought he was showing off for him. If he dared to think anything like that, Kolya would —
“I regard the question as quite a trivial one,” he rapped out again, proudly.

“And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who had not yet spoken, to everyone's surprise. He was quiet and seemed shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, called Kartashov. He was sitting near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified amazement.

The fact was that the identity of the founders of Troy had become a secret for the whole school — a secret that could only be discovered by reading Smaragdov, and no one had Smaragdov except Kolya. One day, when Kolya's back was turned, Kartashov had hurriedly opened Smaragdov, which was lying among Kolya's books, and had immediately hit on the passage about the founding of Troy. That was some time ago, but he had felt uneasy and couldn't bring himself to announce publicly that he too knew who had founded Troy, afraid of what might happen — afraid Krassotkin would somehow put him to shame for it. But now he couldn't resist saying it. For weeks he had been longing to.

“Well, who did found it?” Kolya asked, turning to him with haughty condescension. He could see from his face that Kartashov really did know, and immediately made up his mind how to handle it. There was, so to speak, a discordant note in the general harmony.

“Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius, and Tros,” the boy rapped out at once, and in the same instant he blushed, blushed so deeply it was painful to look at him. But the boys stared at him, stared at him for a whole minute, and then all the staring eyes turned at once and fastened on Kolya, who was still scanning the audacious boy with disdainful composure.
“In what sense did they found it?” he deigned to comment at last. “And what do we mean by founding a city or a state? What is it they do? Did they each go and lay a brick, do you suppose?”
There was laughter. The offending boy turned from pink to crimson. He was silent and on the verge of tears. Kolya held him like that for a minute.

“Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nationality, you first have to understand what you mean by it,” he admonished him in stern, cutting tones. “But I don't attach any consequence to these old wives' tales, and I don't think much of universal history in general,” he added carelessly, addressing the company as a whole.
“Universal history?” the captain asked, looking almost alarmed.

“Yes, universal history. It's the study of the successive follies of mankind and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science,” Kolya said. He was showing off, and he stole a glance at Alyosha — his was the only opinion he was afraid of there. But Alyosha was still silent and serious as before. If Alyosha had said a word, it would have stopped him — but Alyosha was silent and “it might be the silence of contempt,” and that finally irritated Kolya.
“The classical languages, too ... they're simply madness, nothing more. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?”
“I don't agree,” Alyosha said, with a faint smile.

“The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is simply a police measure — that's the sole reason it was introduced into our schools.” By degrees Kolya was starting to get breathless again. “Latin and Greek were introduced because they're a bore and because they dull the intellect. It was dull before, so what could they do to make things duller? It was senseless enough before, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they thought of Greek and Latin. That's my opinion; I hope I never change it,” Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
“That's true,” Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing tone of conviction. He had been listening attentively.
“And yet he's first in Latin himself,” one of the group of boys suddenly cried.
“Yes, father — he says that, and yet he's first in Latin,” Ilusha echoed.

“What of it?” Kolya thought fit to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. “I am slaving away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I'd pass my examination, and I think whatever you do, it's worth doing well. But in my soul I have a profound contempt for the classics and all that fraud ... You don't agree, Karamazov?”
“Why ‘fraud'?” Alyosha smiled again.

“Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn't for the sake of studying the classics that they introduced Latin, but solely as a police measure, to dull the intellect. So what can you call it but a fraud?”
“Why — who taught you all this?” Alyosha cried, surprised at last.

“In the first place, I'm capable of thinking for myself without being taught. Besides, what I just said about the classics being translated — our teacher Kolbasnikov has said the same thing to the whole of the third class.”
“The doctor has come!” cried Nina, who had been silent until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov drove up to the gate. The captain, who had been expecting the doctor all morning, rushed headlong outside to meet him. “Mamma” pulled herself together and assumed a dignified air. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. From her invalid chair Nina anxiously watched him tidy the bed. The boys hurriedly took their leave. Some of them promised to come again in the evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped off the bed.
“I won't go away, I won't go away,” Kolya said hastily to Ilusha. “I'll wait in the passage and come back once the doctor has gone — I'll come back with Perezvon.”

But the doctor had already entered — an important-looking person with long, dark whiskers and a shiny, shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. As he crossed the threshold he stopped, taken aback; he probably thought he had come to the wrong place. “What's this? Where am I?” he muttered, not removing his coat or his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hanging on a line in the corner — all of it puzzled him. The captain, bent double, was bowing low before him.
“It's here, sir, here, sir,” he muttered cringingly. “It's here — you've come to the right place, you were coming to us...”
“Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor said loudly and pompously. “Mr. Snegiryov — is that you?”
“That's me, sir!”
“Ah!”

The doctor looked around the room with a squeamish air once more and threw off his coat, revealing to everyone the grand decoration on his neck. The captain caught the fur coat as it fell, and the doctor took off his cap.
“Where is the patient?” he asked emphatically.
